## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_How quickly does a robot's spatial memory decay into dangerous fiction once moving objects exit the field of view, and how does a machine track what it cannot see?_

Biological organisms navigate dynamic environments effortlessly because their brains maintain persistent spatial representations of objects, surfaces, and obstacles long after direct sensory contact is lost. In contrast, standard vision policies operate almost entirely reactively, processing instantaneous frames and discarding spatial context the moment an object leaves the camera's limited field of view. When an autonomous forklift turns away from a pedestrian, or a mobile manipulator places a tool behind its mast, a memoryless policy behaves as if those physical entities have ceased to exist. Conversely, treating stale observations as permanently static causes robots to plan trajectories around phantom obstacles that have long since moved. A physical AI system requires a spatial memory architecture that bridges this gap: maintaining a persistent 3D representation of the physical world while dynamically modeling epistemic uncertainty and temporal decay. Spatial memory must distinguish between permanent architectural features that remain invariant, dynamic obstacles whose positions evolve along stochastic trajectories, and unobserved regions where uncertainty compounds with elapsed time. This chapter develops the systems architecture for embodied spatial memory, combining voxelized occupancy representations, neural radiance fields, and spatial belief state machines to provide planning algorithms with robust, uncertainty-aware representations of the unobserved world.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Specify the Scene Memory State record (the eighth contract) that unifies discrete belief records with continuous volumetric distance fields, bounding collision query latency under $2\ \mu\text{s}$
- Set belief expiry from bounded uncertainty growth and the task's physical tolerance
- Compare spatial representations (3D Gaussian splatting, NeRFs, octrees, and hashed TSDF/ESDF grids) across the memory footprint vs. query latency frontier
- Design spatial updates that preserve evidence age and distinguish missing observations from verified free space
- Diagnose frozen transforms, phantom tracks, and unobservable drift that pass freshness and innovation checks

:::

## Spatial Belief Persistence and Representation {#sec-memory-preserving-belief}

A memory register can preserve a record exactly while the world it describes moves. As the warehouse mobile manipulator closes on the end of a storage rack, the rack hides the cross aisle from the navigation camera, and whatever the camera last saw there now survives only in memory. A person out of sight past the rack end can walk into the space that record calls empty, and republishing the record with a new software timestamp cannot restore the lost physical evidence. Spatial memory must therefore carry the last measurement time and an error-growth rule into the motion-permission decision.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Observation age and calibrated spatial covariances are generated in @sec-perception-observation-contract.
:::

A physical machine cannot rely solely on raw sensory observations or static memory registers. It requires a **belief**\index{Belief}, an estimate of physical state carried forward from historical sensory evidence, coupled explicitly to an expanding model of uncertainty.[^fn-mem-belief-state] Perception supplies a dated, calibrated observation (as established in @sec-perception-handoff). Spatial memory must determine how long that observation, combined with dynamic motion models, can continue to authorize physical action before uncertainty consumes the machine's remaining clearance.

[^fn-mem-belief-state]: **Belief state formulation**\index{State estimation!belief state}: In a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a belief represents a probability distribution over latent states. A physical state interface additionally carries an error bound. Without the value, frame, evidence epoch, and applicable uncertainty model, a downstream optimizer cannot evaluate clearance during a sensor dropout.

As the second of the four proposal-side stages of Part III, between perception and intent, **spatial memory**\index{Spatial memory} carries geometric and physical state estimates forward across sensor dropouts, occlusions, and variable processing delays. It sits above the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), so a remembered state can shape a proposal but cannot certify its own freshness; the permission path checks the age of the evidence against its own clock.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_sp.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense-Plan belief edge."}
*The Sense $\cap$ Plan belief interface: preserving spatial object state under line-of-sight occlusions.*
:::

In software systems, data age is frequently measured from the instant a message was serialized, published over an inter-process bus, or updated in a shared memory table. In a physical AI system, this convention is dangerous. Propagating a state estimate through an extended Kalman filter at $1\text{ kHz}$ or republishing an $SE(3)$ kinematic transform at $200\text{ Hz}$ creates a stream of fresh software timestamps, but it does not refresh the underlying physical information. The true age of a belief is determined strictly by the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the last physical measurement that constrained it. A downstream tracking loop that reads a position estimate generated by dead reckoning or policy rollouts may observe a publish timestamp only $2\text{ ms}$ old, yet the physical error bound continues to widen at the velocity of the unobserved drift. Timestamping an inference output or a cache lookup records when compute occurred, but it tells the receiver nothing about when reality was last checked.

Consider an industrial mobile robot operating in an active warehouse aisle. As the base turns past a tall pallet rack, the rack's steel uprights occlude the cross aisle from the robot's navigation camera. Immediately after the camera's sightline is cut, the robot's spatial belief about the cross aisle retains low uncertainty ($E_0 \approx 0$). If a human worker or another vehicle was approaching that intersection at walking speed ($1.6\text{ m/s}$), the occluded entity traverses $50\text{ mm}$ of clear space in just $31.25\text{ ms}$—less than two frames at $30\text{ Hz}$. The physical environment does not freeze when a camera loses line of sight. Rather than remaining static, the unobserved entity's uncertainty envelope expands continuously into the planned transit corridor. A stored spatial observation is not an immutable database cache; it is a decaying physical belief whose uncertainty halo inflates over elapsed time $\Delta t$ until it intersects the machine's safety margin.

Memory integrity alone cannot establish geometric validity [@durrant2006simultaneous]. To prevent a machine from acting on stale data, memory systems must treat expiry as an explicit interface event. Each belief carries a deadline, its invalidation horizon (derived in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion), at which its declared error bound reaches the task's physical margin. At that deadline the belief stops supporting motion, and the permission path refuses any proposal that still depends on it and selects a feasible fallback.

A belief that must declare its own expiry has to travel with more than its value, so the first handoff question is what a consumer needs to evaluate a stored value after its sensor loses sight of the object.

## The Spatial Memory Handoff and State Invariants {#sec-memory-handoff}

An unannotated vector such as $[0.142, -0.051, 0.812]$ arriving over a real-time bus conveys nothing about what physical entity is being described, what physical dimension is represented, or how that quantity is scaled. A belief handed to a consumer therefore cannot be a naked array of floating-point numbers. It is a decaying interpretation of physical inputs and must carry its epoch, physical uncertainty, and reference frame to remain usable. A downstream controller receiving raw coordinates without metadata must rely on implicit conventions established at compile time. If an estimator produces positions in meters while an actuator controller expects millimeters, or if an angular rate is mistaken for an absolute orientation, the resulting command registers as a thousandfold tracking error, driving motor current to the actuator thermal limits detailed in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles. To prevent misinterpretation across the causal boundary established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, a belief record must first specify the entity identity, the physical quantity, and the measurement units. The consumer must be able to verify that the value represents the center of mass of a specific workpiece in meters, or the normal contact force on a fingertip in newtons, before routing that number into a control law.

Specifying the quantity and units remains incomplete without binding the value to a concrete reference frame. Identical spatial coordinates describe entirely different physical realities depending on the origin and orientation of the coordinate system. A Cartesian position $[0.142, -0.051, 0.812]\text{ m}$ designates a point suspended in free space when evaluated in the robot base frame\index{Base frame}, but represents a point several hundred millimeters inside a rigid fixture when interpreted in the tool flange frame\index{Tool flange frame}. Because kinematic links flex, joints move, and coordinate transforms update at varying rates, a belief record must carry an explicit frame identifier. Carrying the frame allows the receiving node to look up the corresponding spatial transformation tree and project the stored geometry into the local frame required by the actuator, preventing the controller from acting on geometric misalignments caused by moving kinematic chains.

Geometry and identity describe the physical state at a single moment, but memory must also capture the temporal anchor of that state. The record carries the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the physical interaction or optical exposure that last constrained the estimate. In distributed architectures, intermediate nodes often republish data, execute Kalman filter prediction steps, or run forward kinematic propagations to maintain high-rate control streams, and none of these adds physical evidence. The field must therefore pass unchanged through every republish, filter, and prediction stage, so that consumers measure the age of the information against the physical world rather than against the scheduling frequency of the local computer.

Generating this anchored belief relies on **multi-sensor state estimation**\index{State estimation!contract boundary}\index{Sensor fusion!informational contract}—whether implemented through recursive Extended Kalman Filters (EKF), Unscented Kalman Filters (UKF) [@kalman1960new], or nonlinear factor-graph optimization (Smoothing and Mapping, SAM)—an established mathematical discipline whose operational role is to map asynchronous, heterogeneous sensor observations (such as high-rate IMU accelerations, wheel encoder ticks, and low-rate vision claims) into a minimal sufficient statistic of the plant's latent physical state. The physical AI architecture abstracts the internal numerical mechanics of this fusion pipeline behind the spatial belief contract. Downstream trajectory planning and safety enforcement do not recompute sensor innovation covariances or re-solve factor graphs; they require only that the state estimator provide an unbiased state vector $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, a physically honest uncertainty bound $\mathbf{\Sigma}$, and the true evidence epoch $t_0$ of the measurements that constrained it. The foundational systems requirement is not the choice of filtering algorithm, but the obligation that the estimator model process noise expansion honestly across blind intervals (@sec-appendix-control-covariance derives continuous error covariance propagation) and revoke its validity status whenever physical observability rank collapses (@sec-memory-state-estimation-bounds).

Knowing the evidence epoch $t_0$ establishes elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$, but elapsed time alone cannot determine whether a belief is valid for a given action. Two estimates of identical age diverge at different rates depending on physical constraints. The rack end itself is bolted to the floor, so its remembered position stays within the machine's localization error however long the camera is blind, whereas a person hidden behind it can move at walking speed and spend the same clearance in a few tens of milliseconds.

The minimum record fields necessary for a consumer to evaluate a stored state can be derived directly from the requirement to bound current error. Let $E(\Delta t)$ represent the upper bound of the discrepancy between the stored value and true physical state after an elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$. If an estimator establishes a state at time $t_0$ with an initial uncertainty bound\index{Uncertainty bound} $E_0$, and external disturbances or unmodeled velocities cause the true state to diverge at a maximum rate $r$, the upper bound on error at current time $t$ obeys the linear expansion\index{Error expansion} $E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r\,\Delta t$. At the rack end, $E_0$ is the machine's localization error and $r$ is the walking speed of the person the rack may hide; @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion evaluates that law. Omitting either term leaves the consumer unable to compute $E(\Delta t)$, so an initial bound and an expansion rate are both structurally required fields of the record.

Expressing uncertainty through physical bounds and expansion rates distinguishes a physical AI belief from a probabilistic confidence score. An object detection network might output a class confidence of $0.94$, but that softmax score is not calibrated evidence (@sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities), and a downstream position controller cannot convert a unitless probability into a safe actuator displacement margin (i.e., how far the arm can physically move before risking a collision). A confidence score of $0.94$ provides no information about whether an obstacle boundary is uncertain by $2.0\text{ mm}$ or by $200\text{ mm}$, nor does it indicate how rapidly that boundary moves when occlusion occurs. A physical memory record must express its initial bound $E_0$ and expansion rate $r$ in concrete physical dimensions such as meters, radians, or newtons per second. Furthermore, these rates are valid only within a declared validity region, such as a maximum assumed acceleration or a verified contact friction coefficient. If physical operating conditions leave that region, the expansion rate no longer holds, and the belief record must be treated as invalid.

When memory hands over a tuple containing value, reference frame, evidence epoch $t_0$, initial bound $E_0$, and growth rate $r$, the consumer executes a deterministic verification step before applying the data to physical control. The consumer possesses a task tolerance $E_{\max}$ dictated by the physical task. When the arm guides a gripper finger into the latch-release slot of the cage door, for instance, the slot's clearance sets $E_{\max}$, and positional uncertainty must stay below it. Upon reading the belief record at current time $t_{\text{now}}$, the consumer calculates the elapsed time $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_0$, evaluates the present error bound $E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r \Delta t$, and compares the result directly against $E_{\max}$. Crucially, evaluating this expiry inequality is not a one-time check executed only during path generation. The permission filter evaluates the inequality $E(t_{\text{now}} - t_0) \le E_{\max}$ continuously at the runtime control tick rate ($100\text{--}1{,}000\text{ Hz}$). If an occluded object's error bound breaches clearance mid-trajectory, proposal authority is instantly revoked, forcing an immediate transition to a validated stopping or holding response. If $E(\Delta t) \le E_{\max}$, the belief passes this expiry check and can enter the independent motion-permission check. Otherwise the dependent proposal is refused; the controller selects a validated hold, search, or stop response only when it remains feasible.

::: {#dfn-memory-spatial-belief-contract .callout-definition title="Scene memory state record"}

***Scene Memory State record***\index{Scene Memory State record!definition}\index{Spatial belief record!definition}\index{Belief record!definition} is the formal cyber-physical contract (the eighth in the volume's lineage) emitted by spatial memory. It binds identified physical quantities, discrete entity frames, and continuous volumetric distance fields (TSDF/ESDF) to hardware evidence epochs ($t_0$), estimate epochs ($t_{\text{est}}$), clock synchronization bounds ($\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$), initial uncertainty ($E_0$), continuous error-growth laws ($E(\Delta t)$), operating validity regions, collision query latency budgets ($< 2\ \mu\text{s}$), task clearance expiries ($t_{\text{exp}}$), provenance, and lifecycle status. These fields guarantee that downstream consumers independently evaluate geometric clearance, evidence freshness, and execution deadlines before entering any motion-permission check.

1.  **Significance**: A spatial claim without an error-growth model and hardware evidence epoch cannot be safely evaluated by downstream controllers. As unobserved time elapses ($\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_0$), sensor drift and unmodeled disturbances widen the error bound ($E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r \Delta t$). When that bound exceeds task tolerance ($E(\Delta t) > E_{\max}$), the belief expires, requiring the permission path to refuse dependent proposals and enforce a validated fallback. Simultaneously, continuous volumetric layers must certify sub-2-microsecond ($< 2\ \mu\text{s}$) distance queries to allow reactive 1 kHz reflex loops to verify clearance across dozens of collision hulls.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike unitless classification confidences (such as $P(\text{object}) = 0.94$) or static ROS TF transforms, the Scene Memory State couples metric SI units directly to physical time-decay dynamics, per-cell sensor ray epochs, and hard query execution budgets.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Relying on external middleware publishers to broadcast invalidation signals upon occlusion. If the network drops or an upstream tracking thread hangs, the downstream controller executes open-loop motions on stale beliefs unless it independently evaluates the record's evidence epoch and query budget.

:::

Evaluating the spatial belief record depends on calculating the elapsed time $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_0$ against physical reality. If the consumer cannot verify the exact physical instant when energy transduction occurred, the calculated error bound $E(\Delta t)$ becomes an unanchored fiction, mistaking software compute cycles for physical evidence. The estimate epoch and clock conversion named in the definition exist to protect that anchor, while provenance and lifecycle status, the record's remaining fields, are developed with the schema in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema.

## State Epochs and Temporal Anchoring {#sec-memory-state-epoch}

A pose that leaves an object detector describes where a workpiece was when the camera exposed the frame, not where it is when the message arrives. Every state therefore refers to a specific instant, its **epoch**\index{Epoch}, and a state crossing a physical pipeline carries three of them before a controller can act. The **acquisition epoch**\index{Epoch!acquisition} ($t_0$) is the capture epoch of the observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract), the instant of energy transduction at the causal boundary, such as photons striking a photodiode array or a digital register latching an encoder count, and the belief record carries it as its evidence epoch.[^fn-hw-timer-capture] Memory adds the two epochs that follow it. The **estimate epoch**\index{Epoch!estimate} ($t_{\text{est}}$) marks the instant a state estimator or neural network completed its inference over those measurements and resolved them into a concrete state claim. The **publication epoch**\index{Epoch!publication} ($t_{\text{pub}}$) marks the instant the serialized message was committed to the transport bus for dispatch to downstream consumers.

[^fn-hw-timer-capture]: **Hardware timer input-capture**\index{Hardware!timer input-capture}: Microcontroller timer input-capture channels latch counter values into dedicated shadow registers upon external signal transitions, bypassing operating system interrupt latency. Reading capture registers without atomic synchronization against timer overflow flags causes 16-bit counter aliasing, injecting artificial timestamp jumps equal to the rollover period ($65.5\text{ ms}$ on a $1\text{ MHz}$ timer). In downstream visual-inertial odometry, this temporal discontinuity introduces false acceleration spikes that destabilize platform attitude filters.

Collapsing these three timestamps into a single receipt or transmission timestamp destroys the physical validity of the state. This failure mode is the **publish-time stamping anti-pattern**\index{Publish-time stamping anti-pattern!definition}: many software device drivers populate message timestamp headers with `clock::now()` immediately prior to publishing over the transport bus, rather than latching hardware timer input capture or kernel PTP timestamps. Stamping an inference output or republished message with the current system time hides 20 to 50 milliseconds of camera exposure, direct memory access (DMA) transport, and inference scheduling delay. Downstream state estimators and Kalman filters receive an illusion of temporal freshness while the physical plant has already displaced across space, inducing unmodeled phase lag and trajectory overshoot. That hidden age is displacement at speed, as @sec-perception-photons-to-claims established; for the navigation camera at the base's drive limit, the age at dispatch alone amounts to several centimeters of travel, all of it invisible to a consumer that reads only the publication stamp. A state that records only when data became available tells the consumer nothing about the physical instant the measurement represents, making temporal alignment impossible.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Synchronized hardware timestamping across fieldbuses is established in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

Even when a system records true acquisition epochs, physical AI architectures rely on distributed processing nodes whose local oscillator clocks drift independently. Synchronizing these distributed clocks over standard bus networks introduces a bounded synchronization error, and that temporal uncertainty becomes spatial uncertainty at the relative speed of whatever the record describes.[^fn-hw-ptp-canfd] The observation record of @sec-perception-observation-contract already carries this bound as its clock-conversion error, and a belief built from that observation keeps it. Every consumer adds the bound to the evidence age before judging freshness, and the error budget allocates the distance that bound covers at the record's relative speed alongside sensor resolution and structural deflection.

[^fn-hw-ptp-canfd]: **Fieldbus clock synchronization jitter**\index{Fieldbus!synchronization jitter}: Fieldbus architectures exhibit distinct hardware clock synchronization bounds: IEEE 1588 PTP over Ethernet achieves $\delta t < 1.0\,\mu\text{s}$, EtherCAT Distributed Clocks achieve $<100\text{ ns}$ hardware SYNC0 jitter, and CAN-FD bit-phase synchronization yields $\pm 10\text{--}50\,\mu\text{s}$. Because spatial uncertainty scales with target relative velocity ($e_{\text{sync}} = v_{\text{rel}} \delta t$), microsecond-level synchronization is essential to keep temporal errors within micrometer mechanical budgets. Uncalibrated clock drift between distributed sensor and motor nodes degrades multi-axis tool coordination, inducing high-frequency chatter in joint torque loops.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-epoch-alignment
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE SAMPLING EPOCHS FOR FUSION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-state-epoch (three sensors latch at different epochs).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that fusing two observations requires projecting one across
# │          the gap between their acquisition epochs.
# │ Show:    tactile 12 ms, camera 18.5 ms, encoders 21 ms; camera-to-encoder
# │          gap 2.5 ms.
# │ How:     Illustrative epochs in one cycle; the gap is |t3 - t2|.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

class MemoryEpochAlignment:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    t1 = 12.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (tactile array latches force)
    t2 = 18.5 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (camera finishes integration)
    t3 = 21.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (encoders sample angles)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    gap = abs(t3 - t2).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t1 < t2 < t3, "The illustrative epochs must be in sampling order.")
    check(abs(gap.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, "Camera-to-encoder gap is 2.5 ms.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t1_str = fmt_latency(t1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t2_str = fmt_latency(t2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t3_str = fmt_latency(t3, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gap_str = fmt_latency(gap, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Real physical systems never sample all relevant state variables simultaneously. In an illustrative cycle, a tactile array might latch normal force readings at $t_1 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, an optical tracking camera might finish sensor integration at $t_2 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and joint optical encoders might sample angular positions at $t_3 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str`. These observations occur at different epochs and cannot be combined through direct algebraic operations. Fusing a camera observation at $t_2$ with an encoder observation at $t_3$ requires the consumer to project one state across the temporal gap $\Delta t = |t_3 - t_2| =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` using explicit kinematic models and bounded velocities (for example, propagating the historical camera observation along the joint velocity vector to reconcile it with the instantaneous encoder reading). Without the true acquisition epoch for each individual signal, the alignment calculation cannot determine the sign or magnitude of $\Delta t$. Extrapolating state without an accurate epoch causes the fusion algorithm to compute spatial offsets from fictitious temporal baselines, compounding errors across every fusion cycle.

With these epochs and the clock-synchronization bound carried in the record of @sec-memory-handoff, the consumer computes the elapsed duration between the evidence epoch and the execution deadline, evaluates the worst-case expansion of the error bound, and determines whether the state remains within task tolerances. Handing over a state without its acquisition epoch leaves the consumer blind to transport delays and scheduling jitter, turning deterministic control into open-loop guesswork. Because physical geometry also changes as bodies move through space, spatial transforms between reference frames are subject to the same temporal decay, carrying their own distinct evidence epochs.

## Coordinate Transform Expiry and Calibration Drift {#sec-memory-reference-frames}

A frame binds a coordinate, but in a machine the frame itself moves. @Sec-perception-handoff gave every observation a named frame and related the sensor, body, odometry, and map frames through a transform tree. What the tree does not show is how a transform goes stale. Each edge of the tree in @fig-09-robot-transform-tree stores a rigid-body pose in $SE(3)$\index{Special Euclidean Group $SE(3)$}, parameterized by joint angles [@lynch2017modern; @craig2005introduction], and that pose describes the machine only at the epoch when its geometry was measured. When an onboard computer chains transforms measured at different times, through transport delay, asynchronous sampling, or dropped frames, the product is a hybrid pose the machine never occupied (@sec-appendix-control-kinematics derives the kinematic chain).

A transform also spans several machine words, so a reader racing a writer can see an old rotation paired with a new translation. The seqlock mailbox of @sec-nervous-cadences closes that race without blocking the control thread, because each reader makes one bounded attempt per tick and never waits; a torn read is discarded and the last validated transform ages in its place.

::: {#fig-09-robot-transform-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Manipulator kinematic frame tree and temporal dynamics**: Articulated manipulator geometry (a) and corresponding directed acyclic coordinate transform tree in ROS \\texttt{tf2} (b). Each directed edge stores a homogeneous transformation matrix parameterized by joint state. Composing transforms across disparate acquisition epochs injects lever-arm positioning error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$, while an uncompensated asynchronous edge references stale coordinates (adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013 [@craig2005introduction; @foote2013tf])." fig-alt="Manipulator Kinematic Frame Tree and Temporal Lever-Arm Dynamics. (a) Physical geometry of an articulated manipulator with base link, joint linkages, wrist camera, and tool center point (tool0), indicating lever arm ℓ and angular deflection error e_tool ≈ ℓ · Δθ. (b) Spatial transformation tree (DAG) connecting world reference, base link, kinematic chain link1 through link6, wrist frame, wrist camera, tool0 TCP, and target object, highlighting an asynchronous stale transform edge. (Adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013)."}
![](images/svg/fig09_canonical_robot_frame_tree.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-09-robot-transform-tree, panel (a) illustrates the physical geometry of an articulated serial manipulator carrying an eye-in-hand wrist camera and an end-effector tool center point (`tool0`). Mechanical links (`link1` through `link6`) are connected by revolute joints whose optical encoders continuously sample joint angles $\theta_i(t)$. The tool tip extends beyond the wrist joint by an effective lever arm $\ell$. When the wrist turns at angular rate $\omega$, any temporal latency $\Delta t$ in the wrist coordinate frame introduces an angular lag $\Delta\theta = \omega\,\Delta t$, sweeping the tool tip across an unmodeled circular arc $e_{\text{tool}} \approx \ell\,\Delta\theta$.

Panel (b) depicts the corresponding coordinate transform tree maintained as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in robot middleware such as ROS `tf2` [@foote2013tf]. Each directed edge represents a $4 \times 4$ homogeneous transformation matrix $\mathbf{T}_{A \to B} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ mapping points from child frame $B$ into parent frame $A$. Because internal joint encoders publish at high cadences (typically $500\text{--}1{,}000\text{ Hz}$) over deterministic fieldbuses while external visual perception pipelines publish target poses (`target_object`) at camera framerates ($30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$) over asynchronous network transports, the transform tree inevitably buffers edges with disparate timestamps. If an asynchronous edge (such as `wrist_camera` to `target_object`) drops a frame or stalls, compounding the current robot arm forward kinematics $\mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \to \text{wrist}}(t)$ with a stale vision edge $\mathbf{T}_{\text{wrist} \to \text{object}}(t - \Delta t)$ instantiates the **chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern**\index{Chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern!definition}: synthesizing an unphysical hybrid pose that the robot never occupied.

In robotics middleware like ROS `tf2`, transform listeners resolve coordinate frames by querying the transform tree. When evaluating historical data (for instance, during offline mapping or log replay), the middleware smoothly interpolates between buffered past transforms ($t_1 \le t \le t_2$). At the current control tick $t_{\text{now}}$, however, an active machine operates at the absolute leading edge of time ($t_{\text{now}} > t_{\text{last\_frame}}$). At this leading edge, the transform tree faces the **real-time extrapolation dilemma**: it cannot interpolate into unobserved future frames. The middleware must either block the calling thread until a new frame arrives—violating real-time scheduling deadlines—or extrapolate forward using numerical derivatives, which introduces unconstrained lever-arm rotational error $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$. When communication stalls, naive extrapolation projects kinematic linkages along dead-reckoned arcs that diverge from physical reality.

The cost of an expired transform is direct spatial displacement (@fig-frame-staleness-error). Applying the age-as-displacement relation of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims to kinematics, uncompensated latency translates directly into geometric positioning error through the lever arm of the linkages. For the rigorous cross-product derivation of this kinematic error propagation, see @sec-appendix-control-spatial.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALE SLOT-TO-FINGER TRANSFORM AT THE LATCH SLOT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-reference-frames (lever-arm staleness example); owns
# │          the latch-slot constants that @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion
# │          (LatchSlotBelief) reads.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one missed wrist-camera frame on the slot-to-finger
# │          edge can spend more than the latch-release slot's tolerance, most
# │          of it through the lever arm.
# │ Show:    the frame period, the lateral drift at the finger's drift bound,
# │          the lever-arm arc, and their sum with E0 against the slot.
# │ How:     e_tool ~ E0 + v_drift dt + l omega dt, dt one wrist-camera frame.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchTransformStaleness:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    frame_rate = RM.wrist_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (wrist camera)
    e0 = 0.1 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (finger-to-slot error at the wrist capture)
    v_drift = 12.0 * ureg.millimeter / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (unobserved lateral velocity error bound)
    e_max = 1.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (latch-release slot tolerance)
    lever = 0.15 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (wrist-to-fingertip lever arm)
    omega = 0.30 * ureg.radian / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (wrist rate while aligning the finger)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt = (1 / frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    e_trans = (v_drift * dt).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_rot = (lever * omega * dt / ureg.radian).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_tool = (e0 + e_trans + e_rot).to(ureg.millimeter)
    ratio = (e_tool / e_max).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dt.magnitude - 16.667) < 1e-3, f"Wrist-camera frame period should be 16.7 ms, got {dt}.")
    check(abs(e_trans.magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-6, f"Lateral drift over one frame should be 0.20 mm, got {e_trans}.")
    check(abs(e_rot.magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-6, f"Lever-arm arc should be 0.75 mm, got {e_rot}.")
    check(e_rot > e_trans, "The lever arm must contribute more than the lateral drift.")
    check(e_tool > e_max, "One missed frame must exceed the slot tolerance.")
    check(abs(e_tool.magnitude - 1.05) < 1e-6, f"Total finger error should be 1.05 mm, got {e_tool}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt_str = fmt_latency(dt, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    e0_str = fmt_length(e0, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_drift_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift, unit=ureg.millimeter / ureg.second, precision=0)
    lever_str = fmt_length(lever, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(omega, precision=2)
    e_trans_str = fmt_length(e_trans, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_rot_str = fmt_length(e_rot, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_tool_str = fmt_length(e_tool, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_max_str = fmt_length(e_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    ratio_pct_str = fmt_percent(ratio - 1, precision=0, style="prose")
```

How little staleness it takes to spend a task's tolerance shows at the latch-release slot, while the wrist camera can still see it. Each wrist-camera frame, one every `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.dt_str`, renews the slot's pose in the camera frame and with it the slot-to-finger edge the controller aligns on, and the finger must stay within the slot tolerance $E_{\max}$ of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_max_str`. Suppose that edge misses a single frame. Starting from an initial error of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e0_str`, the finger's lateral offset drifts at most $e_{\text{trans}} = v_{\text{drift}}\,\Delta t$ under an illustrative `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.v_drift_str` bound on its unobserved lateral velocity, validated for the arm's operating region, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_trans_str`. With the fingertip an illustrative $\ell$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.lever_str` beyond the wrist and the wrist turning at an illustrative $\omega$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.omega_str` as it aligns the finger, the lever arm adds $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_rot_str`. The joint encoders measure that turn, but the stale edge still dates the slot to the previous frame while the wrist pose it is composed with is current, so the tree returns a hybrid pose, a finger position the arm never held. Only chaining the slot against the wrist pose of its own capture epoch, or expiring the edge, removes that arc. Left in the chain, the stale edge misplaces the finger by `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool_str`, `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.ratio_pct_str` more than the slot allows, and more of that error comes from the lever arm than from the drift. Because the transform tree evaluates without error, nothing flags the stale pose, and the controller keeps aligning the finger on a slot position that is off by more than the clearance, which on an unfavorable approach puts the finger against the strike plate beside the slot.

::: {#fig-frame-staleness-error fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Transform staleness and lever-arm error at the latch-release slot**: Finger error when the slot-to-finger edge misses one wrist-camera frame of duration $\\Delta t$. Lateral drift at the velocity bound $v_{\\text{drift}}$ moves the finger by $e_{\\text{trans}} = v_{\\text{drift}}\\,\\Delta t$, while the wrist turning at $\\omega$ swings the fingertip, a lever arm $\\ell$ beyond it, by $e_{\\text{rot}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\omega\\,\\Delta t$. Composing the stale edge with the current wrist pose adds both to the initial error $E_0$, so the finger error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx E_0 + e_{\\text{trans}} + \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$ exceeds the slot tolerance $E_{\\max}$." fig-alt="Transform staleness at the latch-release slot. A dashed ghost arm shows the wrist and finger as dated by the stale edge at t0, with a dashed circle marking the slot tolerance E_max around the finger. The current arm at t0 + Δt shows the wrist shifted laterally by e_trans = v_drift Δt and the link of length ℓ turned by Δθ = ω Δt, which swings the finger by e_rot ≈ ℓ Δθ. A red vector from the stale finger position to the current finger, labeled e_tool ≈ E_0 + e_trans + ℓ Δθ, ends well outside the E_max circle."}
![](images/svg/fig09_frame_staleness_error.svg){width="100%"}
:::

To trace this failure mechanism visually, examine the geometric breakdown in @fig-frame-staleness-error. The dashed ghost arm depicts the estimated wrist and finger configuration at time $t_0$, when the slot-to-finger transform was last refreshed by the wrist camera. A dashed circle centered on this initial estimate indicates the mechanical slot tolerance boundary $E_{\max} = 1.0\text{ mm}$; any positioning error remaining inside this circle permits successful mechanical entry. By time $t_0 + \Delta t$, however, one missed camera frame ($\Delta t = 16.7\text{ ms}$) has elapsed. During this interval, unobserved lateral velocity drift moves the wrist translationally by $e_{\text{trans}} = v_{\text{drift}}\,\Delta t = 0.20\text{ mm}$. Simultaneously, wrist rotation at rate $\omega = 0.30\text{ rad/s}$ sweeps the fingertip through angular deflection $\Delta\theta = \omega\,\Delta t = 0.005\text{ rad}$. Operating over the $\ell = 0.15\text{ m}$ lever arm between the wrist pitch axis and the fingertip, this minute angular deflection swings the tool tip by $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\Delta\theta = 0.75\text{ mm}$. Summing the initial uncertainty $E_0 = 0.10\text{ mm}$, the translational drift $e_{\text{trans}} = 0.20\text{ mm}$, and the rotational lever-arm swing $e_{\text{rot}} = 0.75\text{ mm}$ yields a total spatial deflection of $e_{\text{tool}} \approx E_0 + e_{\text{trans}} + \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t = 1.05\text{ mm}$. The solid red vector in @fig-frame-staleness-error pierces the dashed $E_{\max}$ tolerance boundary by 5 percent. Crucially, the kinematic tree computes this forward kinematic composition without reporting an exception, because every individual matrix multiplication is mathematically valid. The control loop remains unaware that it is aligning against a stale virtual target, driving the physical fingertip into the solid aluminum strike plate rather than the entry slot.

::: {#psp-memory-leverage-of-staleness .callout-perspective title="The leverage of staleness"}
*A transform's admissible age is set at the point it serves, not at the joint it measures. The tool point drifts at roughly $v + \ell\omega$, so the longer the lever arm, the sooner an edge expires, and an edge still fresh enough to locate the wrist can be too old to locate the tool center point.*
:::

A transform tree dates the machine's own geometry, and a stale edge misplaces the tool by the motion it missed, amplified by the lever arm. The world around the machine ages in the same way, but it has no joint encoders to report its motion, so memory must also hold the surrounding surfaces and the space between them, and it must record which of that space a sensor has actually seen.

## Certified Spatial Assertions in Scene Memory {#sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers}

Why cannot an embodied robot rely solely on raw, frame-by-frame sensory perception? When an end-to-end policy or reactive planner processes only the instantaneous stream of RGB-D camera frames or point clouds, it suffers from fatal physical vulnerabilities:

1. *Frustum amnesia and limited field of view*: Physical optical sensors possess narrow directional fields of view (typically $60^\circ\text{--}90^\circ$ horizontal aperture). When a mobile manipulator rotates its chassis to navigate an aisle, or turns its wrist to grasp a tool, obstacles that were clearly observed seconds earlier pass outside the camera frustum. A stateless perception pipeline suffers from instantaneous spatial amnesia: an obstacle disappears from the input tensor the moment it leaves the optical cone, inducing destructive collisions if the robot slews, reverses, or extends an arm into that recently observed space.
2. *Occlusion shadows vs. verified free space*: An instantaneous sensor frame provides only a 2.5D surface snapshot from a single vantage point. It cannot distinguish between verified traversable free space and unobserved space occluded in the geometric shadows of foreground obstacles (such as pallet racks or structural uprights).
3. *Rate and latency decoupling for safety reflexes*: Processing high-resolution sensor streams with deep neural networks incurs $30\text{--}100\text{ ms}$ of scheduling and inference latency ($10\text{--}30\text{ Hz}$). In stark contrast, reactive collision filters, Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), and torque reflex loops run synchronously at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$ periods). A 1 ms motor reflex loop cannot stall waiting for a 50 ms neural perception pass.

Persistent 3D spatial memory resolves these bottlenecks by accumulating multi-view observations across physical time into a persistently queryable geometric state. A robot that has swept its range sensor down an aisle holds three kinds of space afterward: space it saw occupied, space it saw empty, and space it never saw. Only the second can ever vouch that a path is clear, and only while its evidence is fresh. Scene memory must balance the physical resolution of obstacles, the memory bandwidth required to update volumetric representations at sensor framerates, and the latency of collision queries executed by high-rate safety controllers. These requirements divide spatial scene memory into three complementary architectural tiers: volumetric metric maps and distance fields, hierarchical dynamic scene graphs, and episodic interaction memory.

### Volumetric metric maps and distance fields {#sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps}

Every metric scene representation stores some version of occupied, free, and unobserved space, but representations differ fundamentally in how they model physical surfaces and what they demand in storage capacity and query latency. Five primary paradigms govern robotic metric memory:

1. **Occupancy Grids and Hierarchical Octrees**: Discretizes 3D space into uniform cubic voxels of side length $r$ [@elfes1989using]. Each voxel cell $m_i$ stores an occupancy probability $P(m_i=1)$, updated recursively in log-odds notation: $L(m_i) = \log [P(m_i=1)/(1-P(m_i=1))]$. Dense grids scale cubically with volume; allocating a $1\text{ m}^3$ workspace at fine $2\text{ mm}$ resolution requires $(1000/2)^3 = 1.25 \times 10^8$ voxels, consuming $125.0\text{ MB/m}^3$ at 1 byte per voxel. To avoid allocating empty volumes, hierarchical octrees (such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap]) group eight sibling voxels recursively, pruning homogeneous free space to achieve compact storage ($0.18\text{--}1.25\text{ MB/m}^3$ at $2\text{--}5\text{ cm}$). However, pointer dereferencing across tree depths introduces CPU cache misses, resulting in query latencies of $24\text{--}38\ \mu\text{s}$.
2. **Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDF)**: Rather than binary occupancy, a TSDF stores the projective distance $d(\mathbf{x})$ from voxel center $\mathbf{x}$ to the nearest observed surface along the sensor sightline [@curless1996volumetric], normalized and truncated to a narrow metric band $[-\delta, +\delta]$: $D(\mathbf{x}) = \min(1, \max(-1, d(\mathbf{x})/\delta))$. Spatial hashing frameworks (such as Voxblox [@oleynikova2017voxblox]) allocate voxel blocks only within the narrow band around perceived surfaces, achieving moderate storage ($4.1\text{ MB/m}^3$ at $5\text{ cm}$) and rapid raycasting ($1.8\ \mu\text{s}$).
3. **Euclidean Signed Distance Fields (ESDF)**: While a TSDF measures distance along optical camera rays, motion planning and reactive obstacle avoidance require the true Euclidean distance to the nearest physical obstacle: $d_E(\mathbf{x}) = \min_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{S}} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|$, with negative signs inside solid geometry. Propagating wave-front expansions across hashed TSDF blocks yields an ESDF. Although maintaining the Euclidean distance field increases memory overhead ($28.5\text{ MB/m}^3$ at $2\text{ cm}$), it delivers sub-microsecond ($0.85\ \mu\text{s}$) distance lookups with analytic continuous clearance repulsion gradients $\nabla d_E(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}^*)/\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}^*\|$, which are essential for trajectory optimization and Control Barrier Functions.
4. **3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)**: Parameterizes geometry as an explicit collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian ellipsoids [@kerbl20233d], each defined by mean position $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{R}^T \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^3$, opacity $\alpha_i \in [0, 1]$, and spherical harmonics color coefficients. By structuring Gaussians in a GPU Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH), 3DGS achieves moderate memory density ($1.6\text{--}5.2\text{ MB/m}^3$) and fast spatial queries ($5.8\text{--}8.2\ \mu\text{s}$) while retaining photographic view-synthesis fidelity.
5. **Implicit Neural Representations (NeRF / Coordinate MLPs)**: Encodes volumetric density $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ and color $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})$ within the stationary weights of a multilayer perceptron (MLP) (e.g., coordinate MLPs such as iMAP or Instant-NGP). While parameterizing an entire room in just megabytes of neural weights yields exceptional memory compression ($0.08\text{ MB/m}^3$), querying signed distance requires evaluating neural network forward passes, imposing latencies exceeding $650\ \mu\text{s}$ per query point.

Analyzing these representations exposes the three foundational physical and systems constraints governing embodied 3D memory: memory footprint scaling, DRAM update bandwidth during sensor ingestion, and collision query latency under hard real-time reflex deadlines.

#### Volumetric memory footprint scaling {.unnumbered}

Consider an operational workspace of physical volume $V_{\text{ws}} = L_x L_y L_z$. Discretizing this domain into cubic voxels of uniform pitch $r$ requires a memory allocation that scales cubically:
$$M_{\text{dense}} = \left(\frac{V_{\text{ws}}}{r^3}\right) S_{\text{voxel}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-dense}
where $S_{\text{voxel}}$ represents the storage footprint per voxel (typically 8 bytes: 4 bytes for 32-bit floating-point distance, 2 bytes for observation weight, and 2 bytes for evidence timestamp). Evaluating @eq-mem-footprint-dense for a warehouse workcell of dimensions $10\text{ m} \times 10\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$ ($V_{\text{ws}} = 300\text{ m}^3$) at fine manipulation resolution ($r = 0.01\text{ m}$, or $1\text{ cm}$) demands $(300 / 0.01^3) \times 8\text{ B} = 3 \times 10^8 \times 8\text{ B} = 2.4\text{ GB}$ of static, contiguous DRAM. On an embedded robot computer, dedicating gigabytes of memory purely to an empty uniform voxel array starves parallel vision backbones and real-time controller memory allocations.

Crucially, physical obstacles do not fill three-dimensional space uniformly; they reside on thin two-dimensional surface manifolds embedded in the workspace ($\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$). Truncating distance fields to a narrow metric band $[-\delta, +\delta]$ around observed surfaces restricts non-trivial distance values to a narrow volumetric shell $V_{\text{band}} \approx 2\delta \cdot A_{\text{surface}}$, where $A_{\text{surface}}$ is the total obstacle surface area. Partitioning space into discrete blocks of $B^3$ voxels (typically $B = 8$, yielding 512 voxels per block) with block physical pitch $L_B = B \cdot r$, the sparse hashed memory footprint obeys:
$$M_{\text{hashed}} = N_{\text{blocks}} \left( B^3 S_{\text{voxel}} + S_{\text{meta}} \right) + N_{\text{buckets}} S_{\text{entry}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-hashed}
where $N_{\text{blocks}} \approx \lceil 2\delta A_{\text{surface}} / (B r)^3 \rceil$, $S_{\text{meta}}$ is the block metadata overhead (spatial coordinates, allocation flags), and $S_{\text{entry}}$ is the hash bucket pointer size. Evaluating @eq-mem-footprint-hashed for the same $300\text{ m}^3$ workcell with an obstacle surface area of $A_{\text{surface}} \approx 120\text{ m}^2$ and narrow band $\delta = 4\text{ cm}$, the active surface volume is only $V_{\text{band}} \approx 9.6\text{ m}^3$. This requires allocating approximately $N_{\text{blocks}} \approx 18{,}750$ blocks, consuming under $77\text{ MB}$ of memory—a 31-fold compression over dense allocation that fits comfortably into processor cache and embedded RAM.

#### Voxel block hashing index mapping {.unnumbered}

To achieve sparse allocation without incurring the pointer traversal overhead of octrees, modern robotic mapping frameworks [@oleynikova2017voxblox] rely on **voxel block hashing**. Continuous world coordinates $\mathbf{x} = [x, y, z]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3$ are mapped to an integer block index $\mathbf{u} = [u_x, u_y, u_z]^\top \in \mathbb{Z}^3$:
$$\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x}}{B \cdot r} \right\rfloor$$ {#eq-mem-block-index}
As formulated in @eq-mem-block-index and @eq-mem-voxel-hashing, the block index is then mapped to a hash table bucket index $h(\mathbf{u}) \in \{0, \dots, N_{\text{buckets}}-1\}$ through spatial XOR hashing:
$$h(\mathbf{u}) = \left( u_x \cdot p_1 \oplus u_y \cdot p_2 \oplus u_z \cdot p_3 \right) \bmod N_{\text{buckets}}$$ {#eq-mem-voxel-hashing}
where $p_1, p_2, p_3$ are large prime constants ($73856093, 19349663, 83492791$) and $\oplus$ denotes bitwise XOR. Inside each allocated block, relative voxel offsets $\Delta \mathbf{u} = \lfloor \mathbf{x}/r \rfloor - B \mathbf{u}$ resolve via direct linear array indexing:
$$\text{offset} = \Delta u_x + B\left(\Delta u_y + B\,\Delta u_z\right)$$
Because each 512-voxel block is laid out contiguously in memory ($512 \times 8\text{ B} = 4{,}096\text{ B}$, matching a standard 4 KB OS virtual memory page), spatial block hashing delivers $O(1)$ block retrieval complexity while ensuring that raycasting traversals and trilinear interpolation kernels achieve near-perfect hardware cache locality on both CPU and GPU architectures.

#### DRAM update bandwidth during ray marching {.unnumbered}

When depth cameras stream range frames at framerate $f_{\text{cam}}$ with $N_{\text{rays}} = W \times H$ pixels per frame, updating the volumetric map requires ray marching from the sensor origin to each observed surface point [@curless1996volumetric]. Each ray traverses a line-of-sight distance $d_{\text{ray}}$ at voxel stepping pitch $r$, requiring $N_{\text{steps}} = d_{\text{ray}} / r$ discrete cell evaluations. The raw DRAM update bandwidth consumed by naive ray marching is:
$$\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = f_{\text{cam}} \cdot N_{\text{rays}} \cdot \left(\frac{d_{\text{ray}}}{r}\right) \cdot S_{\text{rw}}$$ {#eq-mem-dram-bandwidth}
where $S_{\text{rw}}$ is the read-modify-write memory traffic per traversed voxel (typically 8 to 16 bytes for reading current occupancy/distance, updating running weights, and writing back).

Evaluating @eq-mem-dram-bandwidth for a standard VGA depth stream ($640 \times 480 = 307{,}200$ rays) at $f_{\text{cam}} = 30\text{ Hz}$ ray-marched over an average distance of $d_{\text{ray}} = 2.0\text{ m}$ at resolution $r = 2\text{ cm}$ ($100$ steps per ray):
$$\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = 30 \times 307{,}200 \times \left(\frac{2.0}{0.02}\right) \times 8\text{ B} \approx 7.37 \times 10^9\text{ B/s} \approx 7.37\text{ GB/s}$$
On an embedded system on chip (SoC) (such as an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin sharing $102\text{--}204\text{ GB/s}$ of unified LPDDR5 bandwidth between GPU vision models, CPU control threads, and display pipelines), consuming $7.4\text{ GB/s}$ purely on uncoalesced DRAM writes creates severe memory bus contention. Voxel block hashing circumvents this bottleneck by caching active blocks in GPU shared memory or CPU L2 cache and utilizing projective TSDF updates—projecting voxels inside the viewing frustum directly onto the depth image in reverse—collapsing DRAM memory traffic by more than an order of magnitude.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_volumetric_raycasting_bandwidth_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder comparing SoC bus limit against dense TSDF and sparse VDB memory bandwidth."}
*Dense voxel updates saturate the SoC memory bus, requiring sparse VDB caching to protect the control loop.*
:::

#### Collision query latency deadlines for reactive safety filters {.unnumbered}

The choice of metric representation is ultimately dictated not by storage size, but by the hard real-time query latency demanded by physical safety filters. A reactive collision-avoidance reflex loop, such as a Control Barrier Function (CBF) or torque impedance supervisor, executes in a hard real-time loop at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($T_{\text{tick}} = 1{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$). During each 1 ms tick, the safety filter must verify clearance and compute continuous repulsive gradients $\nabla d_E(\mathbf{x}_k)$ across $N_{\text{hulls}}$ collision hulls ($N_{\text{hulls}} = 20\text{--}50$ evaluation spheres distributed along the chassis, articulated links, and gripper fingers). The cumulative collision query latency within a single control tick is:
$$T_{\text{query\_total}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\text{hulls}}} t_{\text{query}}(\mathbf{x}_k) \le T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}$$ {#eq-mem-query-latency-budget}
To leave at least 90 percent of the $1\text{ ms}$ tick for forward kinematics, inverse dynamics, quadratic programming (QP) trajectory optimization, and fieldbus communication, the safety filter allocates at most $T_{\text{reflex\_budget}} = 100\ \mu\text{s}$ to spatial collision checking. Evaluating $N_{\text{hulls}} = 50$ collision hulls imposes a strict per-query latency deadline:
$$t_{\text{query}} \le \frac{T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}}{N_{\text{hulls}}} \approx \frac{100\ \mu\text{s}}{50} = 2.0\ \mu\text{s}$$

This sub-2-microsecond ($< 2\ \mu\text{s}$) deadline governs the viability of spatial representations across the empirical Pareto frontier (@fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto):

- *Hierarchical Octrees (OctoMap)*: Tree traversal from root to leaf across depth $D = \log_2(L/r) \approx 10\text{--}14$ levels requires sequential pointer dereferences. Each tree level introduces CPU cache line misses, yielding query latencies of $24\text{ to } 38\ \mu\text{s}$. For 50 collision hulls, total query time reaches $T_{\text{query\_total}} = 1.2\text{--}1.9\text{ ms}$—exceeding the entire $1\text{ ms}$ control tick and triggering fatal real-time deadline misses that drop motor actuation packets.
- *Implicit Neural Representations (NeRF / Coordinate MLPs)*: While coordinate MLPs compress an entire room into megabytes of neural weights, querying signed distance requires evaluating a forward pass through multi-layer perceptrons ($t_{\text{query}} \approx 650\ \mu\text{s}$). Evaluating 50 hulls sequentially would consume $32.5\text{ ms}$, throttling the control loop to under $30\text{ Hz}$ and introducing catastrophic phase lag. Consequently, implicit fields remain confined to offline deliberators.
- *Hashed TSDF / ESDF Grids (Voxblox)*: By combining $O(1)$ spatial block hashing with continuous trilinear interpolation inside contiguous memory, hashed distance fields deliver per-query latencies of $t_{\text{query}} = 0.85\ \mu\text{s}$ (ESDF) to $1.8\ \mu\text{s}$ (TSDF). Evaluating 50 collision hulls completes in $42.5\ \mu\text{s}$, well within the $100\ \mu\text{s}$ safety budget and enabling certified 1 kHz reflex loops.

The choice of metric representation defines an empirical Pareto trade-off between volumetric memory footprint and spatial collision query latency (@fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto). Continuous trajectory optimization and real-time reflex controllers running in 1 kHz control loops ($1{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$ periods) require spatial clearance and gradient queries to execute in under $10\ \mu\text{s}$ across dozens of robot body articulation points. While implicit neural representations achieve minimal memory density, their forward-pass query latency confines them to deliberative offline planners. Conversely, hashed ESDFs and dense occupancy arrays trade higher memory footprints for the sub-microsecond query speeds required by real-time safety filters.

::: {#fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**3D scene representation frontier: memory footprint vs. spatial query latency**: Empirical Pareto trade-off across implicit neural fields, hierarchical octrees, 3D Gaussian splatting, and hashed voxel grids. While implicit coordinate MLPs compress rooms into megabytes of weights, multi-layer forward passes exceed real-time collision query limits ($>100\\ \\mu\\text{s}$). Hashed voxel grids (Voxblox TSDF/ESDF [@oleynikova2017voxblox]) consume $4.1\\text{--}28.5\\ \\text{MB/m}^3$ but provide the sub-microsecond query latencies ($<2\\ \\mu\\text{s}$) necessary to service 1 kHz reactive control loops." fig-alt="Log-log scatter plot of volumetric memory footprint in megabytes per cubic meter vs. spatial point distance and collision query latency in microseconds. The empirical Pareto frontier descends from iMAP NeRF (0.08 MB/m3, 650 us) through OctoMap 5cm (0.18 MB/m3, 24 us), 3DGS Compressed Scaffold (1.6 MB/m3, 8.2 us), Voxblox TSDF (4.1 MB/m3, 1.8 us), Voxblox ESDF (28.5 MB/m3, 0.85 us), to Dense Occupancy Array 2 mm Grid (125 MB/m3, 0.45 us). Shaded green region highlights the real-time 1 kHz control budget below 10 us, and shaded red region indicates the deliberative zone above 100 us."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14.0, 8.2), dpi=300, facecolor="#FFFFFF")
ax.set_facecolor("#FFFFFF")
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, linestyle="--", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5, color="#E2E8F0")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)

# 1. Shaded Region for Real-Time Control Clearance
ax.axhspan(0.2, 10.0, color="#ECFDF5", alpha=0.55, zorder=1)
```

:::

To interpret the system-level design space in @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto, observe the axes plotted on logarithmic scales. The horizontal axis measures volumetric memory footprint in megabytes per cubic meter ($\text{MB/m}^3$) of operational space, spanning from sparse coordinate MLPs ($0.08\text{ MB/m}^3$) to dense millimeter voxel grids ($125.0\text{ MB/m}^3$). The vertical axis measures spatial point collision and distance query latency in microseconds ($\mu\text{s}$), spanning from sub-microsecond array lookups ($0.45\ \mu\text{s}$) to neural forward passes ($650\ \mu\text{s}$). The blue dashed curve traces the empirical Pareto frontier across four orders of magnitude in query latency.

Two operational regimes govern this landscape:

- *Real-Time 1 kHz Control Budget (Shaded Green Region, $<10\ \mu\text{s}$):* A reactive reflex loop operating at $1\text{ kHz}$ has a strict tick budget of $1{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$. When evaluating clearance across 20 to 50 spherical collision hulls distributed along a manipulator arm, the safety filter must bound total collision query time to under $100\ \mu\text{s}$, demanding a per-query latency strictly below $2\ \mu\text{s}$ (@eq-mem-query-latency-budget). Hashed ESDF ($0.85\ \mu\text{s}$), TSDF ($1.8\ \mu\text{s}$), and dense uniform voxel arrays ($0.45\ \mu\text{s}$) fall squarely within this sub-2-microsecond contract budget, whereas 3DGS BVH queries ($5.8\text{--}8.2\ \mu\text{s}$) require reducing hull counts or running at lower cadences.
- *Deliberative Offline Zone (Shaded Red Region, $>100\ \mu\text{s}$):* Implicit coordinate MLPs such as NeRF and iMAP achieve extraordinary parameter efficiency, compressing an entire room into under $10\text{ MB}$ of weight storage. However, querying occupancy or signed distance requires evaluating a forward pass through multiple fully connected layers for every individual point. Evaluating 50 collision points sequentially would consume over $32.5\text{ ms}$, throttling control cadence to under $30\text{ Hz}$ and introducing dangerous phase lag. Consequently, implicit representations remain confined to global semantic map synthesis and offline deliberators.
- *The Hierarchical Middle Ground:* OctoMap ($24\text{--}38\ \mu\text{s}$) compresses empty space effectively ($0.18\text{--}1.25\text{ MB/m}^3$), but pointer traversal across octree depths incurs CPU cache misses that place it outside the $1\text{ kHz}$ reflex envelope, making it suitable for intermediate $10\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$ global motion planners.

What a map can certify comes from how a range return updates it. Traversing the ray from the sensor to the return [@amanatides1987fast], the map asserts **negative evidence**\index{Negative evidence} in every cell the ray crossed and positive evidence in the cell where it ended; @sec-appendix-ml-voxels gives the log-odds update. Negative evidence lets the map retire a phantom obstacle as soon as the same region is seen empty, instead of waiting for a timeout, and it also marks the limit of what the map can say. It covers only cells a valid ray actually traversed. It says nothing about the volume behind the return, and a new scan down the aisle cannot renew a cell hidden behind the rack, so the occluded cross aisle stays unknown and still needs expiry. Every return also touches every cell along its ray, so sparse allocation saves capacity but not traversal, and that traffic reaches the permission path only as added evidence age (@sec-placement-resource-contention).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_active_negative_evidence_chain.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Causal chain showing raycast through free space to surface hit, evicting ghost obstacles."}

*Active negative evidence along sightlines clears phantom obstacles without waiting for timeout decay.*
:::

Because negative evidence renews only the cells a ray crossed, a map's publication time dates none of its cells, so the manifest in @tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief carries evidence epochs per cell. Those epochs are not free, because every allocated cell stores its own timestamps beside its occupancy estimate, and they belong in the map's memory budget for the same reason the value does. Furthermore, to service reactive 1 kHz control barrier filters evaluating dozens of body collision hulls, the volumetric layer must bound distance and gradient query latency to under $2\ \mu\text{s}$ (as achieved by hashed TSDF/ESDF implementations). A motion consumer checks the query budget, evidence age, and state of every cell its path uses, including cells marked unknown, and derives conservative clearance from a separately validated layer.

| Map field                                 | Unit or type                         | Meaning and consumer check                                                                      |
|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `voxel_grid_origin`, `voxel_resolution_m` | m; m                                 | Spatial anchor and pitch; match the active frame and calibration                                |
| `map_update_epoch`                        | capture-clock ns                     | Last map publication/update; **not** freshness of every cell                                    |
| `cell_evidence_epoch`                     | capture-clock ns per cell            | Last physical observation for that cell; never refreshed by prediction or unrelated map updates |
| `free_space_sweep_epoch`                  | capture-clock ns per occupancy cell  | Last valid observed free ray through that cell                                                  |
| `clock_conversion`, `sync_error_ns`       | mapping; ns                          | Convert capture epochs to the consumer's monotonic clock with bounded error                     |
| `query_latency_budget_us`                 | $\mu\text{s}$ ($\le 2\ \mu\text{s}$) | Bound collision and distance gradient query time to preserve 1 kHz reactive control loops       |

: **Volumetric belief manifest and cell evidence**: The map header describes layout, query latency budget, and update time, while cell-local acquisition epochs determine whether the particular path region is fresh. The consumer treats unobserved or expired cells as unknown unless a separately validated policy permits traversal. {#tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief tbl-colwidths="[26,22,52]"}

### Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graphs {#sec-memory-hierarchical-scene-graphs}

Semantic memory sits above the metric layer and inherits its limits. Beyond raw metric volumes and radiance fields, foundation-model-driven physical AI requires spatial memory to organize space into semantic hierarchies. The **3D dynamic scene graph (DSG)**\index{3D dynamic scene graph}, formulated by @rosinol2021kimera in Kimera and extended by @hughes2022hydra in Hydra, bridges metric SLAM with symbolic reasoning by structuring spatial memory into a five-layer hierarchical graph (@fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph):

1. *Metric-Semantic Mesh (Layer 1):* High-resolution triangular mesh capturing fine surface geometry with vertex semantic labels.
2. *Object and Agent Nodes (Layer 2):* Bounded 3D geometric entities with oriented bounding boxes, visual embeddings, and tracked dynamic trajectories.
3. *Places and Freespace Topology (Layer 3):* 3D Voronoi topology and navigable freespace clearance spheres ($p_i$) for planning collision-free paths.
4. *Rooms and Structural Enclosures (Layer 4):* Functional architectural subdivisions partitioned by semantic walls and portals.
5. *Buildings and Global Topology (Layer 5):* Top-level semantic graph governing long-horizon mission allocation.

::: {#fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture**: Five-layer spatio-temporal memory organization bridging metric SLAM to symbolic foundation reasoning. Layer 1 captures triangular metric mesh geometry; Layer 2 extracts 3D objects and dynamic agents; Layer 3 models topological places via Voronoi freespace clearance spheres ($p_i$); Layer 4 structures architectural rooms and portals; and Layer 5 establishes global building mission topology. Vertical inter-layer edges coordinate upward abstraction (compressing metric surfaces into symbolic entities) and downward grounding (translating task tokens into metric coordinates) (adapted from Rosinol et al. [@rosinol2021kimera] and Hughes et al. [@hughes2022hydra])." fig-alt="Hierarchical five-layer 3D Dynamic Scene Graph architecture. From bottom to top: Layer 1 Metric Mesh surface geometry, Layer 2 Objects and Agents with support relations, Layer 3 Places with Voronoi freespace clearance spheres, Layer 4 Rooms connected by portals, and Layer 5 Buildings with global topology. Side arrows depict upward Abstraction and downward Grounding across tiers."}
![](images/svg/fig09_dynamic_scene_graph_hierarchy.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph, memory is structured as a five-tier hierarchy that bridges low-level metric reconstruction with high-level symbolic task planning:

- *Layer 1 (Metric-Semantic Mesh):* Represents continuous physical surfaces as dense triangular meshes with per-vertex semantic class labels and surface normal vectors, providing the geometric foundation for physical collision avoidance.
- *Layer 2 (Objects and Dynamic Agents):* Clusters mesh vertices into discrete rigid entities bounded by 3D oriented bounding boxes (OBBs), carrying categorical labels, 6-DoF poses, and tracked dynamic velocity vectors.
- *Layer 3 (Places and Freespace Topology):* Constructs a generalized Voronoi diagram of navigable free space, parameterizing corridors as topological clearance spheres $p_i = (\mathbf{x}_i, r_i)$ where center $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and radius $r_i$ bounds the maximum obstacle-free sphere.
- *Layer 4 (Rooms and Architectural Enclosures):* Groups topological place nodes into functional structural zones (e.g., aisles, storage bays, charging docks) separated by physical boundaries and passable doorways.
- *Layer 5 (Buildings and Global Mission Topology):* Synthesizes top-level semantic topology connecting floors, buildings, and outdoor zones for multi-agent dispatch and long-horizon route scheduling.

The operational power of this structure stems from bidirectional cross-layer communication:

- *Upward Abstraction:* Raw sensor depth frames generating millions of mesh vertices in Layer 1 are progressively summarized into dozens of object nodes in Layer 2 and a handful of room nodes in Layer 4. This collapses memory bandwidth by three orders of magnitude, allowing an on-chassis vision-language-action model to reason over multi-room environments without overflowing its KV cache.
- *Downward Grounding:* When a high-level mission token targets a specific semantic object (such as "latch handle in Bay 3"), the system traverses downward: Layer 5 resolves Bay 3, Layer 4 locates the target storage enclosure, Layer 3 plans a topological route through freespace spheres, Layer 2 extracts the object's 6-DoF coordinate frame, and Layer 1 evaluates real-time metric clearance against the localized triangular mesh.

### Episodic memory and physical interaction history {#sec-memory-episodic}

While metric voxel grids and dynamic scene graphs maintain spatial persistence—answering *where* objects and free space exist—physical AI agents require **episodic memory**\index{Episodic memory} to record causal history: answering *what happened*, *when it occurred*, and *what physical consequences resulted*. Rather than acting as a passive diagnostic flight recorder or write-only disk log, episodic memory functions as an active, queryable index structured around hybrid automaton transitions, contact events, and tool engagements across multi-minute task horizons.

An episodic memory store in physical AI is structured around three foundational primitives:

1. **Multimodal Interaction Traces**: An episodic trace records an immutable, time-indexed stream of state-action tuples $\tau_k = (t_k, \mathbf{s}_k, \mathbf{a}_k, \mathbf{o}_k, \mathbf{w}_k)$, where $t_k$ is the monotonic capture epoch, $\mathbf{s}_k$ is the estimated kinematic state, $\mathbf{a}_k$ is the executed actuator command, $\mathbf{o}_k$ is the visual observation snapshot, and $\mathbf{w}_k = (\mathbf{f}_k, \boldsymbol{\tau}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^6$ is the high-bandwidth contact wrench measured at the wrist force-torque sensor. Recording wrench signatures alongside kinematic trajectories allows the agent to diagnose unobservable failures (such as slippage, micro-collisions, or latch binding) that leave no trace in visual scene memory.
2. **Action-Event Anchors**: Storing uninterrupted high-frequency telemetry ($1\text{ kHz}$ wrench data and $30\text{ Hz}$ video) rapidly exhausts edge LPDDR5 bandwidth and NVMe storage. Episodic memory manages this deluge by segmenting continuous execution into discrete *action-event anchors*. An anchor is instantiated whenever the physical interaction state experiences a discrete hybrid automaton transition: a sudden rise in normal contact force ($F_n > F_{\text{contact}}$), a gripper switch state change, an unexpected velocity stall ($\|\dot{\mathbf{q}}\| \approx 0$ under active motor effort), or a human operator intervention. Each anchor retains high-resolution telemetry in a localized temporal buffer ($[-500\text{ ms}, +500\text{ ms}]$) around the transition while compressing steady-state transit into low-frequency summary vectors.
3. **Keyframe Context Eviction and Freshness Decay**: When an autoregressive policy or deliberative agent conditions on prior episodic history, its attention context length is strictly bounded by hardware memory limits. In classical NLP, streaming attention evicts older tokens via sliding-window FIFO buffers [@xiao2024streamingllm]. In physical AI, however, FIFO eviction is hazardous: a naive FIFO policy evicts the critical visual observation of a closed latch or a colleague entering a blind aisle simply because dozens of intervening navigation steps consumed the context budget. Physical episodic memory instead implements **saliency-weighted keyframe retention**: event anchors marking mechanical state transitions are pinned to non-volatile belief slots with explicit evidence epochs, while repetitive geometric observations are evicted as fresh metric returns renew the local voxel map.

By decoupling spatial geometry (held in metric TSDF/ESDF layers) from causal interaction history (held in episodic action-event anchors), physical AI systems preserve both the metric clearances needed for immediate collision avoidance and the temporal provenance required for long-horizon task recovery.

A learned policy's context is memory of a different kind. An autoregressive policy holds its recent observations in a key-value cache whose growth @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline derives, and a **streaming window**\index{Streaming ring-buffer attention} bounds that cache by evicting its oldest tokens [@xiao2024streamingllm], whether or not their physical consequences have ended. A person seen stepping behind the rack before the window began is gone from the context but not from the aisle. A physical fact the machine must still honor therefore lives in a belief record with its own evidence epoch, never only in the policy's context.

For motion permission, then, a representation without an epoch is an unverified assertion, and an estimate whose error bound exceeds task tolerance must be excluded from motion proposals before the permission path considers actuator commands. The machine cannot halt every operation at the first missed frame, however. Extending action across brief sensing gaps requires estimators that propagate belief forward until new measurements arrive to confirm or correct the state.

## Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay {#sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion}

When direct sensing fails due to occlusions, sensor blind spots, or lighting dropouts, a physical AI system cannot simply freeze its actuators. It must rely on an internal predictive transition model to propagate its spatial belief forward across the unobserved interval. A recursive Kalman filter\index{Filter!Kalman} propagates states through kinematic equations of motion and process noise covariances,[^fn-hist-bayesian-filter] while a learned generative policy predicts future states autoregressively\index{Network!autoregressive}.

Crucially, prediction extrapolates old evidence forward without renewing it, as @sec-memory-preserving-belief established. While forward propagation preserves the utility of an observation by accounting for anticipated velocities and forces, it does not reset the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the underlying physical measurement.
